articles.title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
articles.summary: Hamas says the kites found in Israeli border communities in recent days were launched by children in Gaza.
articles.body:
Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory.

Several kites were found in an Israeli community near the border with Gaza over the weekend, local media reported.

"Forceful actions will be taken to put an end to this phenomenon," Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday.

Before the war, kites and balloons carrying incendiary devices were launched into Israel, causing fires that burned forest and farmland.

Hamas has denied responsibility for the new kites - which were not carrying explosives - and said they belonged to "children searching for their innocent childhood amid the rubble".

The group also accused Israel of using the kites as a "pretext" for continued air strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed last October.

UK, Canada and Australia condemn Israel for refusing criminal probe into aid worker killings in Gaza Published 4 days ago

UK, Canada and Australia condemn Israel for refusing criminal probe into aid worker killings in Gaza

Israel confirms soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed and opens criminal investigation Published 5 days ago

Israel confirms soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed and opens criminal investigation

Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza Published 6 days ago

Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza

Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media.

The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response.

No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said.

But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives."

Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security."

Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps".

"These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added.

On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza.

A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media.

The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand.

"There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace."

On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah.

The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

articles.title: 'Their faces burnt': Disturbing details emerge in Bangladesh Hindu family murder
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city, with investigators uncovering disturbing details abou.
articles.body: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city, with investigators uncovering disturbing details about the killings and an alleged attempt to destroy evidence.The victims were identified as retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their 23-year-old daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty. Their bodies were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area at around 11.30pm on Saturday.According to Bangladeshâs The Daily Star, Pritilataâs younger sister Puja Chakraborty said the family noticed that the victimsâ faces had been burnt when the bodies were handed over to them.âWhen we received the bodies in the evening, we found that their faces had been burned. Earlier, police did not allow us to go near the bodies,â Puja said.Sumit Chowdhury, acting superintendent of police of CID Rangpur, told The Daily Star that investigators suspected a flammable substance had been used on the victimsâ faces.âThe killers appear to have poured a flammable substance on the victimsâ faces either before or after killing them. At this stage, we cannot say what substance was used. The investigating officer will collect samples and send them to the CID forensic department for examination. We will know more once the test results are available.âThe bodies were found in different parts of the house. The mother and daughter were found on the staircase, Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof, while Priyam was found under a bed. Police initially suspected that the family had been strangled, with the killings believed to have taken place between midnight on Thursday and early Friday.Investigators said suspects Mugdha and Siddhartha allegedly remained inside the house after the killings. According to Prothom Alo, they reportedly bathed there, ate dates and cucumbers from the refrigerator and used yaba before leaving on Friday during Jummah prayers, when the streets were relatively quiet.Police also found cupboards and drawers opened and belongings scattered, suggesting an attempt to make the killings appear to be a robbery. Evidence allegedly indicated an attempt to test a gold bangle using fire, while two phones belonging to the victims had been submerged in water mixed with detergent, apparently to destroy evidence.The suspects were detained based on these clues and allegedly confessed during questioning, police said. Gold jewellery believed to have been stolen was later recovered from an abandoned location they identified. Date pits found inside the house have also been sent for DNA testing, according to Prothom Alo.Puja said the family had not been heard from since Thursday and all four phones were switched off. Police later broke open the locked main gate and found the bodies.Police, CID and Detective Branch teams are jointly investigating the case, while preparations were under way to file a murder case.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Shelley Fabares, ‘Johnny Angel’ singer and actor on ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ dies at 82
articles.summary: Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said. No cause was given.
articles.body: Shelley Fabares, an actor who was a fixture on television for decades from her days as a young teenager on “The Donna Reed Show,” through “One Day at a Time” and “Coach,” has died. She was 82. She died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said in a statement to The Associated Press. No cause was given. “To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort,” her family wrote. “She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for.” Fabares was born in Santa Monica, California, in 1944, and started acting as a young child. Her first television credit came at age 10 when she appeared on “The Loretta Young Show.” Many movies and television shows followed: She acted with Paul Newman, Frank Sinatra and Eva Marie Saint in a Producers Showcase production of “Our Town” and was in the Rosalind Russell movie “The Girl Rush” and the Rock Hudson drama “Never Say Goodbye.” Other early credits include “Annette,” “Captain Midnight” and the “Black Leather Jackets” episode of “The Twilight Zone.” Her biggest break came when she was cast as Mary Stone on “The Donna Reed Show,” where she was a regular from 1958 through 1963. During that time she also got a recording contract and had two Top 40 hits, including “Johnny Angel.” In the early 1960s, she also co-starred in three movies with Elvis Presley: “Girl Happy,” “Spinout” and “Clambake.” “I think the years on ‘The Donna Reed Show,’ the years from 14 to 19, were so incredibly important,” Fabares told the Los Angeles Times in 1993. “Donna Reed was simply an extraordinary woman, a woman of great strength, kindness, integrity and compassion. I am not trying to make her sound like a saint, but she had the most profound influence on me. I carry her with me today.” In the late 1970s, Fabares made an impression as Francine Webster on the CBS sitcom “One Day at a Time.” She also played James Caan’s wife in “Brian’s Song.” One of her biggest roles came when she was cast as Christine Armstrong in “Coach,” although the show took a minute to find its audience. “I did always feel from the very beginning if they could find the right spot for us, this was a show that would last,” she said in the 1993 Los Angeles Times interview. Fabares married twice, first to producer Lou Adler in 1964. She had been married to “M-A-S-H” actor Mike Farrell since 1984. She was also a devoted advocate for Alzheimer’s awareness, which affected her mother. In early 1999, a visit to the emergency room for an esophageal bleed revealed that she had progressive liver failure. After spending 22 months on a waiting list, she had liver transplant surgery in October 2000. In an interview with Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles three years after the transplant, she said she’d been “changed by the experience” and was eternally grateful to Farrell, who was with her “every step of the way.” Her family, in their statement, said that “we will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives.”

articles.title: Royal Shakespeare Company backs plan for £600m theme park near Bicester
articles.summary: A company submitted a planning application for the attraction in the Oxfordshire countryside last year.
articles.body:
The Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) has backed plans to build a £600m history-based theme park in the Oxfordshire countryside.

French firm Puy du Fou submitted proposals to build the site, north of Bicester, to Cherwell District Council last year.

The RSC described the proposal as an "exciting opportunity to further enhance the UK's cultural and tourism offer".

Puy du Fou has said it aims to open the park in phases, beginning in 2029 and that it would employ about 2,000 people. Its plans have sparked concerns from some locals, who have expressed fears about the impact the site will have on things such as traffic and wildlife.

A new group has also been created to bring together representatives from Heyford Park and surrounding villages to discuss the impact of major schemes planned in the area, including the theme park.

The forum, approved by Oxfordshire County Council, wants to help prevent the area from "descending into traffic gridlock".

But Blenheim Palace , national tourism agency VisitBritain , performing arts and entertainment trade union Equity , and Experience Oxfordshire, are among those who have previously backed the theme park plan.

The Puy du Fou attraction would include four period villages and 13 live shows in which visitors could "immerse themselves in British history".

Developers estimate the attraction could welcome up to 1.4 million visitors a year once fully open.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

In a letter seen by the BBC, issued by the RSC's senior leadership team to the council, and confirmed by the organisation as authentic, it said: "We recognise the important role that major cultural and visitor attractions can play in strengthening the regional economy, increasing tourism, creating employment opportunities, and encouraging wider participation in arts, culture, and heritage.

"There is currently no equivalent attraction operating at this scale within the UK, and we can see the potential for the project to attract new visitors to the region, generate economic activity, and contribute to the continued growth of the visitor economy across the Midlands and surrounding areas."

The letter said the RSC was "particularly encouraged by the potential for collaboration across the cultural, tourism, hospitality, and education sectors".

"Major attractions often act as catalysts for wider partnerships, helping organisations work together to create richer visitor experiences and strengthen the overall appeal of a destination," it added.

The RSC concluded that it supported the "ambitions" of the project and the "potential benefits it could bring to the region, its communities, and the wider visitor economy".

Puy du Fou has had history-themed parks in Les Epesses in France since 1978 and in Toledo, Spain, since 2021.

articles.title: Why Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in West Bank are pogroms
articles.summary: Waves of settler attacks, aided by Israel’s military, increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom.
articles.body:
Attacks on Palestinian communities by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, which are often supported by Israeli forces, have gathered pace over the past month since settlers from the Havat Gilad settlement attacked Palestinian homes on the eastern edge of Tal, southwest of Nablus.

On Sunday and Monday, the Israeli military raided multiple towns, villages and refugee camps across the occupied territory, and reports of arrests, home searches and settler attacks have continued to mount.

A 15-day siege on three families comprising 15 people, including two children, in the village of Qusra, which is ongoing, drew a rare public condemnation this month from the United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and its West Bank settlements.

Israel is also pushing ahead with plans for the so-called E1 settlement expansion close to Jerusalem, which human rights organisations warn would essentially sever the West Bank in two, further hampering the freedom of movement of Palestinians on either side of it and endangering the possibility of a Palestinian state.

The West Bank attacks increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom, experts said. United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese described these Israeli attacks against Palestinians as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”.

So why are experts calling settler attacks pogroms, and do they fit the formal definition of one?

Settlers, frequently supported by the Israeli military, have been attacking Palestinian homes, businesses and farmland across the West Bank. Such attacks have been commonplace for decades as settlements have expanded across the territory, but they have gathered pace after October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza. The attacks in the West Bank have become particularly violent and frequent over the past month.

Israeli settlements and outposts across the West Bank are illegal under international law.

According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli settlers now number roughly 780,000 across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. They live in 192 settlements and 400 outposts, making up 71 percent of Area C in the West Bank, which is under full Israeli civil and military control, and 91 percent of the Jordan Valley, the commission said.

Settlers often set up outposts without formal approval around Palestinian villages from which they launch a campaign of harassment, including killing and stealing livestock; cutting off water, electricity and supplies; and damaging property to drive local residents out. Once they establish a more formal settlement, they often receive retrospective approval from the Israeli government for the settlement.

In some places more recently, settlers have laid siege to individual family homes, such as in the Ras al-Ein area of Qusra , cutting off water and other supplies and damaging orchards or harming livestock.

This has set a new pattern: Settlers establish a tent adjacent to individual homes; Palestinians’ homes are besieged with essentials cut off; and Israeli soldiers arrive, not to remove the settlers but rather to remove the family – through arrests or for their “protection”.

In Qusra, the three besieged families were forced together into one of the family houses. Meanwhile, Israeli forces have occupied one of the other homes for use as a military post and thrown furniture and belongings from its windows, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day and marking the fastest pace since the agency began systematic tracking two decades ago.

Separately, a UN-appointed commission of inquiry has found that the Israeli authorities have repeatedly failed to prevent foreseeable settler attacks and, in some cases, have directly enabled them through army protection and the provision of weapons and funding.

OCHA has found that settler attacks, demolitions and evictions forcibly displaced more Palestinians in the first four months of this year than in the whole of 2025.

OCHA reported that 107 communities, comprising 5,900 Palestinians, had been completely or partially displaced as a result of settler violence since January 2023. It also found that the Israeli military has expelled another 32,000 Palestinians from their homes in the West Bank since January 2025, essentially emptying the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps.

Major dictionaries in the US and United Kingdom vary to some degree on the definition.

The British Collins Dictionary identifies a pogrom as “organised, official violence against a group of people for racial or religious reasons” with a notable inclusion of official, or state-backed, violence.

The Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary calls it “the organised killing of large numbers of people, because of their race or religion” without mention of state-sanctioned violence.

Merriam-Webster says it is “an organised massacre of helpless people” – “specifically: such as a massacre of Jews”.

Cambridge Dictionary says it is “an act of organised cruel behaviour or killing that is done to a large group of people because of their race or religion”.

The word is understood to have been introduced via Yiddish and was at first used to describe the wave of violent, organised mob attacks on Jewish communities in the Russian Empire after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881.

It is important to note that unlike legal terms, including “crimes against humanity” or “genocide”, “pogrom” has no established legal definition under international law.

Can attacks in the West Bank be referred to as pogroms?

Besides UN Special Rapporteur Albanese, who has described Israeli attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”, Israeli officials themselves have described such attacks as “pogroms”.

On February 26, 2023, hundreds of Israeli settlers attacked Huwara and surrounding Palestinian communities after two Israeli settlers were killed. A Palestinian was killed, hundreds were injured, and homes, businesses and cars were burned.

The Israeli military’s then-commander in the West Bank, Yehuda Fuchs, called the settler attacks a “pogrom”, and it was also recorded as such by the US Department of State .

The Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem has also previously described Israeli actions in the West Bank as “pogroms”, especially after the February 2023 attacks. Later, it followed up with a report titled, The Pogroms Are Working – the Transfer Is Already Happening, which argued that settler attacks were contributing to the displacement of Palestinian communities.

“Settler violence is not a new phenomenon, but over the past three years, it has become more violent, more systematic and, most importantly, part of a state mechanism intended to ethnically cleanse large parts of the West Bank,” said Yair Dvir, the spokesperson for B’Tselem.

“The government funds and arms the settlers while the Israeli military stands by and, in many cases, actively participates in the attacks,” he told Al Jazeera. “So far, these militias have expelled 64 Palestinian communities and taken control of around 1 million dunams [100,000 hectares/247,100 acres] of land.”

Dvir also told Al Jazeera that the Israeli settlers are “now carrying out organised attacks on established Palestinian villages and towns in order to drive out their residents”.

“These are armed militias operating as an unofficial arm of the state with a shared goal: to ethnically cleanse as much of the West Bank as possible,” he added.

The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention – which is named after Polish Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who is credited with coining the term genocide after the Holocaust – referred to settler attacks on al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village in the Ramallah and el-Bireh governorate, as “pogroms”, reporting that hundreds of armed settlers attacked residents and burned buildings and cars while soldiers stood by this year. In 2025, the Israeli military uprooted thousands of Palestinian olive trees in al-Mughayyir.

Raheel Dhattiwala, an Indian scholar who focuses on collective violence, told Al Jazeera: “West Bank attacks fit the characteristics of a pogrom – systematic targeting of one civilian group by another with state approval. A few senior Israeli army officers have called it ‘pogroms’ in the past too, for example after attacks in Huwara.

“One might want to debate the use of the term ‘pogrom’, but it is accurate to call settler violence systematic attacks of occupiers with government approval on groups of occupied people.”

articles.title: Democrats demand Iran war cost details from Trump, Hegseth
articles.summary: Nearly 50 House Democrats reportedly signed a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for more details on the cost of the Iran war. “What was billed as a two-week operation is now a full-scale war that has lasted for over 150 days, cost over $37 billion, and claimed the lives of…
articles.body:
Nearly 50 House Democrats reportedly signed a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for more details on the cost of the Iran war .

“What was billed as a two-week operation is now a full-scale war that has lasted for over 150 days, cost over $37 billion, and claimed the lives of 18 servicemembers,” the House Democrats wrote in the letter . “At the same time, prices across the country have gone up significantly, placing the burden of this conflict on American families.”

Democratic Reps. Jason Crow (Colo.), Maggie Goodlander (N.H.) and Derek Tran (Calif.) led the charge on the letter, per NBC. The trio served in the military and co-chair House Democrats’ national security task force.

“The Iranian regime — which for 47 years has chanted ‘Death to America’ and threatened our troops overseas — can never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon, and the President’s team will continue to communicate with Congress as we work toward this shared goal,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told The Hill.

Trump initially said the Iran war would take roughly a month, but the conflict has stretched on for nearly six months without a lasting peace deal between his administration and Iranian leaders. The administration on Monday is ramping up its economic offensive against Iran.

In late July, Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee the conflict had cost roughly $37.5 billion. When reached for comment on the letter from House Democrats, a Pentagon official referred The Hill to that price tag.

But NBC News reported earlier that month the Pentagon’s internal cost estimate of the war was $80 billion to $100 billion when accounting for the costs of repairing damaged military bases, replacing destroyed aircraft and fully replenishing weapons stockpiles.

White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought also asked Congress for $67.1 billion in June for the Pentagon. That included $1.7 billion for readiness, $17.3 billion for operational costs and $21 billion for munitions. The military has depleted its weapons stockpiles during the Middle Eastern conflict.

The war has come with financial costs for Americans, particularly due to the Iranian military’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.09 as of Monday , up from less than $3 two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the conflict, according to AAA.

“It is unconscionable that the Administration is asking for more to fund the very thing that is raising costs for Americans,” the letter from the four dozen lawmakers added, referencing the White House’s supplemental funding request. “The Administration should be focused on ending the conflict and addressing the very real financial concerns of the American public.”

Trump said earlier this month it is worth it for Americans “to pay a tiny, little bit more” for gas so the U.S. military could ensure Iran cannot develop a nuclear weapon.

“So remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK. … I’ll never apologize, I did the right thing,” the president said at an event in Garden City, N.Y.

The Democratic lawmakers asked Trump and Hegseth for a “public, comprehensive assessment” of the economic impact of the war by Sept. 11.

That assessment, the representatives noted, should include all Pentagon operational costs, the impact on oil and energy markets and the macroeconomic effects imposed by the war, such as its impact on gross domestic product growth (GDP), inflation and supply chains.

Annual inflation has risen from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July , as measured by the consumer price index .

U.S. GDP also increased at an annual rate of 1.5 percent in the second quarter after 2.1 percent growth in the first quarter, based on data released by the Bureau of Economic Analysis .

articles.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
articles.summary: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.body:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.

While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable.

Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.

The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.

What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.

El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.

El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries .

This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further.

"The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton.

"All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added.

The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.

The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.

Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas.

The oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat trapped by humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels.

"The latest Copernicus data reinforce the troubling upward trend in ocean temperatures,” said Smyth.

Warmer seas help to fuel more extreme weather. They can provide storms with extra moisture and energy, and can intensify heatwaves on land in some coastal regions by reducing the cooling effect of sea breezes.

Warmer water also takes up more space, raising sea levels and bringing a greater risk of coastal flooding - while intense ocean heat can be devastating for sea habitats, such as coral reefs.

The increasing frequency of marine heatwaves is already "putting increasing pressure on marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them", Burgess said.

articles.title: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board
articles.summary: Last year the organisation African Parks  admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

articles.title: Meet Finley Holz, the Minnesota student who studied 10 years of wolf-tracking data and found deep snow can make wolves move less

articles.body: Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locations and converted them into movement data, while a Python programme helped compare movements with weather conditions. His research found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. The study recorded a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and movement.However, cold snaps did not significantly affect how much the wolves moved. The research also produced an unexpected finding. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level. Holz's project was recognised in a Minnesota Story Map competition, where he placed second.How Finley Holz used wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movementHolz combined wolf-tracking information with winter weather measurements, including high and low temperatures, snow depth and snowfall events.The project used ArcGIS Pro to organise shapefiles and create maps showing wolf locations. The resulting location points were then converted into movement data. Holz also wrote a Python programme to align the wolf movements with the different winter weather conditions.The data came from wolf collar information provided by the Fond du Lac Resource Management Division. Pine Knot News, a Minnesota-based publication, reports that wildlife programme manager Michael Schrage provided wolf collar data and guidance to the students. Holz and other students also had the opportunity to collar Otter Creek wolf pups on the Fond du Lac Reservation on 5 May.Deep snow was linked to reduced wolf movement in MinnesotaOne of the clearest findings from Holz's research was the relationship between snow depth and wolf movement. According to the project published in Fairfolio, titled âThe Effect of Winter Weather Events on Wolf (Canis lupus) Movement on the Fond du Lac Reservationâ, Holz's second hypothesis was supported: wolves moved less as snow depth increased. The study found a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement. In simple terms, the data showed that as the snow became deeper, the distance wolves travelled per movement decreased.The finding in similar terms, stating that Holz "found that winter cold snaps have no effect on wolf movement" but that there was "a negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement: the deeper the snow, the less the wolves moved." Holz had also expected extreme cold to affect wolf movement. His third hypothesis predicted that wolves would move the least during a cold snap. However, the results did not support this idea. The Fairfolio project says there was no difference in wolf movement during a cold snap compared with normal winter movement. That meant that extremely cold periods, at least within the conditions examined in the study, did not produce the reduction in movement Holz had expected.Finley Holz found wolf movement decreased as winter storms approachedAnother unexpected finding came from the relationship between wolf movement and winter storms. Holz originally hypothesised that wolves would travel the furthest immediately after a storm. Instead, the data showed that their movement declined around the time of a storm.According to the project abstract, "Three days after the storm had passed, the wolves moved significantly less than the average winter movement (pFinley Holzâs wolf research earns second place in Minnesota Story Map competitionHolz's wolf research also became part of a successful Minnesota Story Map competition. Two Cloquet High School students and a Hermantown student with Cloquet connections won the top three places in the competition. Hermantown freshman Gabriel Bradley came first, while Cloquet sophomores Finley Holz and Melanie Buhs placed second and third.The Minnesota Alliance for Geographic Education competition challenges students to conduct research and present their findings through an ArcGIS Online story map.Holz's project focused on the effect of winter weather events on wolf movement, while Bradley's project examined factors affecting wolf pack den relocation.Minnesota studentâs decade-long wolf research reveals effects of snow and stormsHolz's project provides a detailed look at how winter conditions can influence wolf movement in northeastern Minnesota. Rather than finding that every form of severe winter weather caused wolves to travel less, the research showed a more specific pattern. Increasing snow depth was associated with reduced wolf movement, while cold snaps alone did not significantly change movement.The study also raised a new question about how wolves respond to approaching storms. articles.title: 'I was living paycheck to paychek': Woman says coming back to India from UK after 4 years not happiest decision but right one for nervous system
articles.summary: UK News: At a time when students outside India are in a fix to decide whether going back to India would be a better decision because of immigration bottlenecks.
articles.body: At a time when students outside India are in a fix to decide whether going back to India would be a better decision because of immigration bottlenecks, Arshiya Mahajan, an Indian woman shared her experience of coming back to India after living four years in the UK. Mahajan said it was not 100% the happiest decision she ever made but it felt like the right one for the nervous system as living in the UK was becoming a lot less living and more about maintaining a life, she said."Visa paperwork. Rental issues. Immigration timelines. Money. What happens when friends move away. What my next job should be. Whether I could actually afford the life I was living," she said, listing out the factors that worried her."I was living increasingly paycheck to paycheck, occasionally needing my family to help me out, while simultaneously trying to convince myself that I was âdoing fine," she wrote, adding that she was more in survival mode financially, professionally, socially and also mentally.Mahajan said she won't say her life in the UK was a failure, but it made her able to go back to India. "I got to travel more than I ever imagined, meet people from all over the world, become much more independent and grow professionally in ways I probably couldnât have anticipated. The UK gave me a lot," she said."For now, being back in India has been good for me. Thereâs still a lot Iâm processing, and Iâm sure Iâll have moments of wondering whether I made the right decision. But Iâm increasingly convinced that not every good decision has to feel euphoric," she said.Reactions to the 'back to India' postSuch 'back to India' social media posts always get some racist comments and there was no exception here too.
